questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $2.00 \text{ kg}$ travelling at a speed of $10.0 \text{ m/s}$ accelerates at $3.00 \text{ m/s}^2$ for $5.00 \text{ s}$. Determine its final kinetic energy.
questions.solution:
Given initial velocity $u = 10.0 \text{ m/s}$, acceleration $a = 3.00 \text{ m/s}^2$, and time $t = 5.00 \text{ s}$.

Using the first equation of motion, the final velocity $v$ is:

$v = u + at$

$v = 10.0 + (3.00)(5.00) = 25.0 \text{ m/s}$

The final kinetic energy $K$ is given by:

$K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$

$K = \dfrac{1}{2}(2.00)(25.0)^2$

$K = 625 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A box is pushed a distance of $4.0 \text{ m}$ across a floor which offers a resistance of $100 \text{ N}$. What is the work done by the resisting force?
questions.solution:
Work done is given by the dot product of force and displacement vectors, $W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{d} = F d \cos(\theta)$.

The resisting force acts in the direction opposite to the displacement, so the angle between them is $\theta = 180^{\circ}$.

Given $F = 100 \text{ N}$ and $d = 4.0 \text{ m}$.

$W = 100 \times 4.0 \times \cos(180^{\circ})$

$W = 400 \times (-1) = -400 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The combined mass of a cyclist and the bike is $90 \text{ kg}$. Determine the increase in kinetic energy when the speed increases from $6.0 \text{ km/h}$ to $12 \text{ km/h}$.
questions.solution:
Initial speed $v_1 = 6.0 \text{ km/h} = 6.0 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m/s} = \dfrac{5}{3} \text{ m/s}$

Final speed $v_2 = 12 \text{ km/h} = 12 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m/s} = \dfrac{10}{3} \text{ m/s}$

Initial kinetic energy $K_1 = \dfrac{1}{2} m v_1^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 90 \times \left(\dfrac{5}{3}\right)^2 = 45 \times \dfrac{25}{9} = 125 \text{ J}$

Final kinetic energy $K_2 = \dfrac{1}{2} m v_2^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 90 \times \left(\dfrac{10}{3}\right)^2 = 45 \times \dfrac{100}{9} = 500 \text{ J}$

Increase in kinetic energy $\Delta K = K_2 - K_1 = 500 - 125 = 375 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $5.0 \text{ kg}$ slides down an incline having an inclination of $30^\circ$ and a length of $10 \text{ m}$. Determine the work done by the force of gravity.
questions.solution:
Mass of the block, $m = 5.0 \text{ kg}$

Length of the incline, $s = 10 \text{ m}$

Angle of inclination, $\theta = 30^\circ$

Vertical height moved by the block, $h = s \sin\theta = 10 \sin 30^\circ = 10 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 5 \text{ m}$

Work done by the force of gravity is given by $W = mgh$

Taking $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$,

$W = 5.0 \times 9.8 \times 5 = 245 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A stationary particle of mass $15 \text{ g}$ is accelerated by a constant force of $2.50 \text{ N}$ over a displacement of $2.50 \text{ m}$. Determine the work done and the average power delivered.
questions.solution:
Work done by the constant force is given by:

$W = Fs = 2.50 \times 2.50 = 6.25 \text{ J}$

Acceleration of the particle is:

$a = \dfrac{F}{m} = \dfrac{2.50}{15 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{500}{3} \text{ m/s}^2$

Using the equation of motion $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with $u = 0$:

$v^2 = 0 + 2 \times \dfrac{500}{3} \times 2.50 = \dfrac{2500}{3}$

$v = \dfrac{50}{\sqrt{3}} \text{ m/s}$

For constant acceleration, the average velocity is:

$v_{avg} = \dfrac{u+v}{2} = \dfrac{25}{\sqrt{3}} \text{ m/s}$

Average power delivered is:

$P_{avg} = F \times v_{avg} = 2.50 \times \dfrac{25}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{62.5}{\sqrt{3}} \approx 36.1 \text{ W}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle travels from a position $\vec{r}_1 = (2 \text{ m})\hat{i} + (3 \text{ m})\hat{j}$ to a new position $\vec{r}_2 = (3 \text{ m})\hat{i} + (2 \text{ m})\hat{j}$ while experiencing a force $\vec{F} = (5 \text{ N})\hat{i} + (5 \text{ N})\hat{j}$. Determine the work done by this force on the particle over the displacement.
questions.solution:
The displacement vector of the particle is given by:

$\Delta\vec{r} = \vec{r}_2 - \vec{r}_1$

$\Delta\vec{r} = (3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j}) - (2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j})$

$\Delta\vec{r} = \hat{i} - \hat{j} \text{ m}$

The work done by the constant force is the dot product of the force and the displacement:

$W = \vec{F} \cdot \Delta\vec{r}$

$W = (5\hat{i} + 5\hat{j}) \cdot (\hat{i} - \hat{j})$

$W = (5)(1) + (5)(-1)$

$W = 5 - 5 = 0 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A man travels along a straight horizontal road carrying a block of mass $2 \text{ kg}$ in his hand. If he covers a distance of $40 \text{ m}$ with an acceleration of $0.5 \text{ m/s}^2$, determine the work done by the man on the block during the motion.
questions.solution:
Mass of the block, $m = 2 \text{ kg}$

Acceleration of the block, $a = 0.5 \text{ m/s}^2$

Displacement of the block, $s = 40 \text{ m}$

The force exerted by the man on the block has two components: a vertical component to balance the weight of the block and a horizontal component to provide the acceleration.

The vertical force is $F_y = mg$. The work done by this force is zero because it is perpendicular to the horizontal displacement.

The horizontal force is $F_x = ma$. The work done by this force is given by $W = F_x s = mas$.

Substituting the given values:

$W = 2 \times 0.5 \times 40 = 40 \text{ J}$

Alternatively, using the work-energy theorem, the work done by the net force is equal to the change in kinetic energy of the block:

$W = \Delta K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - \dfrac{1}{2}mu^2$

Using the equation of motion $v^2 - u^2 = 2as$:

$W = \dfrac{1}{2}m(2as) = mas = 2 \times 0.5 \times 40 = 40 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle is acted upon by a force $F = a + bx$ in the $x$-direction, where $a$ and $b$ are constants. Determine the work done by this force during a displacement from $x = 0$ to $x = d$.
questions.solution:
The work done by a variable force $F$ during a displacement from $x_1$ to $x_2$ is given by $W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F \, dx$.

Given $F = a + bx$, $x_1 = 0$, and $x_2 = d$.

Substituting the values into the work integral:

$W = \int_{0}^{d} (a + bx) \, dx$

$W = \left[ ax + \dfrac{1}{2}bx^2 \right]_{0}^{d}$

$W = ad + \dfrac{1}{2}bd^2$

$W = \left(a + \dfrac{1}{2}bd\right)d$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $250 \text{ g}$ slides down an incline of inclination $37^\circ$ at a uniform speed. Determine the work done against friction as the block covers a distance of $1.0 \text{ m}$.
questions.solution:
Since the block moves with a uniform speed, its acceleration is zero. Thus, the net force acting on the block along the incline is zero.

The component of gravitational force down the incline is balanced by the frictional force acting up the incline.

$f = mg \sin \theta$

Work done against friction as the block moves a distance $d$ is given by:

$W = f \times d = mg \sin \theta \times d$

Substituting the given values ($m = 0.25 \text{ kg}$, $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$, $\theta = 37^\circ$, $d = 1.0 \text{ m}$):

$W = 0.25 \times 10 \times \sin(37^\circ) \times 1.0$

$W = 2.5 \times \dfrac{3}{5} = 1.5 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $m$ is positioned on another block of mass $M$, and the two-block system rests on a horizontal surface. When a constant horizontal force $F$ is applied to the lower block, it generates an acceleration of $\dfrac{F}{2(m+M)}$ in the system, and the two blocks travel together continuously. Calculate the frictional force acting on the smaller block.
questions.solution:
Given that the two blocks move together, they share the same acceleration. The acceleration of the system is given by:

$a = \dfrac{F}{2(m+M)}$

For the smaller block of mass $m$, the only horizontal force acting on it is the static frictional force $f$ provided by the lower block. This frictional force is responsible for its acceleration.

Applying Newton's second law to the smaller block:

$f = ma$

Substituting the value of acceleration $a$ into the equation, we get:

$f = m \left[ \dfrac{F}{2(m+M)} \right]$

$f = \dfrac{mF}{2(m+M)}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $m$ is placed upon another block of mass $M$, and the system rests on a horizontal surface as depicted in the figure. A constant horizontal force $F$ exerted on the lower block yields an acceleration of $\dfrac{F}{2(m+M)}$ for the system, with both blocks always moving together. Determine the coefficient of kinetic friction between the larger block and the horizontal surface.
questions.solution:
Since both blocks move together, they can be considered as a single system of total mass $(M+m)$.

The normal force exerted by the horizontal surface on the system is $N = (M+m)g$.

The kinetic friction force acting on the lower block from the surface is $f_k = \mu_k N = \mu_k(M+m)g$.

Applying Newton's second law to the system in the horizontal direction:

$F - f_k = (M+m)a$

Substituting the given acceleration $a = \dfrac{F}{2(M+m)}$ into the equation:

$F - \mu_k(M+m)g = (M+m) \left( \dfrac{F}{2(M+m)} \right)$

$F - \mu_k(M+m)g = \dfrac{F}{2}$

Rearranging the terms to solve for $\mu_k$:

$\mu_k(M+m)g = F - \dfrac{F}{2} = \dfrac{F}{2}$

$\mu_k = \dfrac{F}{2(M+m)g}$

A constant horizontal force $F$ exerted on the lower block yields an acceleration of $\dfrac{F}{2(m+M)}$ for the system, with both blocks always moving together. Determine the coefficient of kinetic friction between the larger block and the horizontal surface.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $m$ sits on top of another block of mass $M$, and the entire system rests on a horizontal surface. A constant horizontal force $F$ acting on the lower block results in an acceleration of $\dfrac{F}{2(m+M)}$ for the system, where the two blocks consistently move together. Evaluate the work done by the force of friction on the smaller block by the larger block over a displacement $d$ of the system.
questions.solution:
Given that the two blocks move together, they share the same acceleration. The acceleration of the system is given as:

$a = \dfrac{F}{2(m+M)}$

For the smaller block of mass $m$, the only horizontal force acting on it is the static friction force $f$ exerted by the larger block $M$. This friction force is responsible for the acceleration of the smaller block.

Using Newton's second law for the smaller block:

$f = ma$

Substituting the value of acceleration $a$:

$f = m \left( \dfrac{F}{2(m+M)} \right) = \dfrac{mF}{2(m+M)}$

The displacement of the system, and thus the smaller block, is $d$ in the direction of the acceleration (and the friction force).

The work done by the force of friction on the smaller block is:

$W = f \cdot d$

$W = \left( \dfrac{mF}{2(m+M)} \right) d = \dfrac{mFd}{2(m+M)}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A box weighing $2000 \text{ N}$ is to be slowly slid a distance of $20 \text{ m}$ along a straight track. The coefficient of friction between the box and the track is $0.2$. Determine the work done by a person who pulls the box using a chain oriented at an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal.
questions.solution:
Let $T$ be the tension in the chain and $N$ be the normal reaction.

Since the box is slid slowly, the net force on it is zero.

Balancing the forces in the vertical direction:

$N + T \sin\theta = mg$

$N = mg - T \sin\theta$

Balancing the forces in the horizontal direction:

$T \cos\theta = \mu N$

Substituting the value of $N$:

$T \cos\theta = \mu (mg - T \sin\theta)$

$T \cos\theta + \mu T \sin\theta = \mu mg$

$T \cos\theta (1 + \mu \tan\theta) = \mu mg$

$T \cos\theta = \dfrac{\mu mg}{1 + \mu \tan\theta}$

The work done by the person is the work done by the tension force over the distance $d$:

$W = (T \cos\theta) d$

Substituting $mg = 2000 \text{ N}$, $d = 20 \text{ m}$, and $\mu = 0.2$:

$W = \dfrac{0.2 \times 2000 \times 20}{1 + 0.2 \tan\theta}$

$W = \dfrac{8000}{1 + \dfrac{\tan\theta}{5}}$

$W = \dfrac{40000}{5 + \tan\theta} \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A box weighing $2000 \text{ N}$ is to be slowly slid a distance of $20 \text{ m}$ along a straight track. The coefficient of friction between the box and the track is $0.2$. A person pulls the box using a chain oriented at an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal. Compute the work done if the person chooses the value of $\theta$ that minimizes the magnitude of the pulling force.
questions.solution:
Let $F$ be the pulling force applied at an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal. For the box to slide slowly, the net force on it must be zero.

Resolving forces horizontally and vertically:

$F \cos\theta = \mu N$

$N + F \sin\theta = W$

Substituting $N = W - F \sin\theta$ into the first equation:

$F \cos\theta = \mu (W - F \sin\theta)$

$F (\cos\theta + \mu \sin\theta) = \mu W$

$F = \dfrac{\mu W}{\cos\theta + \mu \sin\theta}$

To minimize the pulling force $F$, the denominator $\cos\theta + \mu \sin\theta$ must be maximized. Taking the derivative with respect to $\theta$ and equating to zero:

$-\sin\theta + \mu \cos\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \tan\theta = \mu$

For $\tan\theta = \mu$, we have $\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+\mu^2}}$ and $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\mu}{\sqrt{1+\mu^2}}$.

The minimum force is:

$F_{min} = \dfrac{\mu W}{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+\mu^2}} + \dfrac{\mu^2}{\sqrt{1+\mu^2}}} = \dfrac{\mu W}{\sqrt{1+\mu^2}}$

The work done by the person is the work done by the pulling force:

$W_{done} = F_{min} d \cos\theta$

$W_{done} = \left(\dfrac{\mu W}{\sqrt{1+\mu^2}}\right) d \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+\mu^2}}\right) = \dfrac{\mu W d}{1+\mu^2}$

Substituting the given values $\mu = 0.2$, $W = 2000 \text{ N}$, and $d = 20 \text{ m}$:

$W_{done} = \dfrac{0.2 \times 2000 \times 20}{1 + (0.2)^2} = \dfrac{8000}{1.04}$

$W_{done} = \dfrac{8000}{1.04} \approx 7692 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A person slowly slides a block of weight $100 \text{ N}$ up a smooth incline of inclination $37^\circ$. If the driving force is applied parallel to the incline, determine the work done by the person in moving the block through a distance of $2.0 \text{ m}$.
questions.solution:
Weight of the block, $mg = 100 \text{ N}$

Inclination of the plane, $\theta = 37^\circ$

Distance moved, $s = 2.0 \text{ m}$

Since the block is moved slowly, the net force on the block is zero. The driving force $F$ applied by the person balances the component of gravity along the incline.

$F = mg \sin \theta$

$F = 100 \sin 37^\circ = 100 \times \dfrac{3}{5} = 60 \text{ N}$

Work done by the person is the work done by the driving force.

$W = Fs = 60 \times 2.0 = 120 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A person slowly slides a block of weight $100 \text{ N}$ up a smooth incline of inclination $37^\circ$. If the driving force is applied in the horizontal direction, determine the work done by the person in moving the block through a distance of $2.0 \text{ m}$.
questions.solution:
Let the horizontal driving force applied by the person be $F$.

Since the block is moved slowly, its acceleration is zero. The net force along the incline must be zero. Equating the components of the driving force and the weight along the incline:

$F \cos \theta = W \sin \theta$

The work done by the person is the work done by the horizontal force $F$ over the displacement $s$ along the incline. The angle between the horizontal force and the displacement is $\theta$:

$W_{\text{person}} = F s \cos \theta$

Substituting $F \cos \theta = W \sin \theta$ into the work equation:

$W_{\text{person}} = (W \sin \theta) s = W s \sin \theta$

Given $W = 100 \text{ N}$, $s = 2.0 \text{ m}$, and $\theta = 37^\circ$:

$W_{\text{person}} = 100 \times 2.0 \times \sin 37^\circ$

$W_{\text{person}} = 200 \times \dfrac{3}{5} = 120 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the average frictional force required to bring a car weighing $500 \text{ kg}$ to a halt over a distance of $25 \text{ m}$, given that its initial speed is $72 \text{ km/h}$.
questions.solution:
Initial velocity $u = 72 \text{ km/h} = 72 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m/s} = 20 \text{ m/s}$

Final velocity $v = 0$

Distance $s = 25 \text{ m}$

Mass $m = 500 \text{ kg}$

Using the work-energy theorem:

Work done by friction = Change in kinetic energy

$-F \times s = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - \dfrac{1}{2}mu^2$

$-F \times 25 = 0 - \dfrac{1}{2} \times 500 \times (20)^2$

$-25F = -250 \times 400$

$25F = 100000$

$F = 4000 \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the average force required to accelerate a $500 \text{ kg}$ car from rest to $72 \text{ km/h}$ over a distance of $25 \text{ m}$.
questions.solution:
Given mass of the car, $m = 500 \text{ kg}$

Initial velocity, $u = 0$

Final velocity, $v = 72 \text{ km/h} = 72 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m/s} = 20 \text{ m/s}$

Distance covered, $s = 25 \text{ m}$

Using the equation of motion $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$:

$(20)^2 = 0 + 2a(25)$

$400 = 50a$

$a = 8 \text{ m/s}^2$

The average force required is given by Newton's second law:

$F = ma$

$F = 500 \times 8 = 4000 \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of mass $m$ travels on a straight line, with its velocity varying with the distance travelled according to the equation $v = a\sqrt{x}$, where $a$ is a constant. Determine the total work done by all the forces during a displacement from $x = 0$ to $x = d$.
questions.solution:
According to the work-energy theorem, the total work done by all forces is equal to the change in kinetic energy of the particle.

$W = K_f - K_i$

Given the velocity equation $v = a\sqrt{x}$.

At $x = 0$, the initial velocity is $v_i = 0$, so the initial kinetic energy is $K_i = 0$.

At $x = d$, the final velocity is $v_f = a\sqrt{d}$.

The final kinetic energy is $K_f = \dfrac{1}{2} m v_f^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} m (a\sqrt{d})^2 = \dfrac{m a^2 d}{2}$.

Therefore, the total work done is $W = \dfrac{m a^2 d}{2} - 0 = \dfrac{m a^2 d}{2}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $2.0 \text{ kg}$ initially at rest on an inclined plane of inclination $37^\circ$ is pulled up the plane by a constant force of $20 \text{ N}$ applied parallel to the incline. The force acts for one second. If the work done by the applied force is $40 \text{ J}$, compute the work done by the force of gravity in that one second. Take $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
Given the work done by the applied force $W_F = 40 \text{ J}$ and the applied force $F = 20 \text{ N}$.

The displacement of the block along the incline is given by:

$s = \dfrac{W_F}{F} = \dfrac{40}{20} = 2 \text{ m}$

The block moves $2 \text{ m}$ up the incline. The vertical displacement of the block is $h = s \sin 37^\circ$.

The work done by the force of gravity is negative since the displacement is upwards while gravity acts downwards:

$W_g = -mgh = -mgs \sin 37^\circ$

Substituting the given values ($m = 2.0 \text{ kg}$, $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$, $\sin 37^\circ = \dfrac{3}{5}$):

$W_g = -2.0 \times 10 \times 2 \times \dfrac{3}{5}$

$W_g = -12 \times 2 = -24 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $2.0 \text{ kg}$ initially at rest on an inclined plane of inclination $37^\circ$ is pulled up the plane by a constant force of $20 \text{ N}$ applied parallel to the incline. The force acts for one second. Determine the maximum possible work done by the applied force during this time. Take $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
The work done by the applied force is $W = Fs$, where $F = 20 \text{ N}$ and $s$ is the displacement of the block along the incline in $1 \text{ s}$.

To maximize the work done, the displacement $s$ must be maximum, which requires the acceleration $a$ of the block to be maximum.

The forces acting on the block along the incline are the applied force $F$ upwards, the gravitational component $mg \sin 37^\circ$ downwards, and the frictional force $f$ downwards.

The equation of motion is $F - mg \sin 37^\circ - f = ma$.

For maximum acceleration, the frictional force must be zero ($f = 0$).

Substituting the given values:

$20 - 2.0 \times 10 \times \sin 37^\circ = 2.0 \times a$

$20 - 20 \times \dfrac{3}{5} = 2.0 a$

$20 - 12 = 2.0 a \Rightarrow a = 4 \text{ m/s}^2$

The maximum displacement in $t = 1 \text{ s}$ starting from rest is:

$s = \dfrac{1}{2} a t^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times (1)^2 = 2 \text{ m}$

The maximum possible work done by the applied force is:

$W = Fs = 20 \times 2 = 40 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $2.0 \text{ kg}$ initially at rest on an inclined plane of inclination $37^\circ$ is pulled up the plane by a constant force of $20 \text{ N}$ applied parallel to the incline. The force acts for one second. If the work done by the applied force is $40 \text{ J}$, determine the kinetic energy of the block at the instant the force ceases to act. Take $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
Given the applied force $F = 20 \text{ N}$ and the work done by this force $W = 40 \text{ J}$.

The displacement $s$ of the block along the incline can be calculated as:

$W = Fs \Rightarrow 40 = 20s \Rightarrow s = 2 \text{ m}$

Using the kinematic equation $s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$ with initial velocity $u = 0$ and time $t = 1 \text{ s}$:

$2 = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2}a(1)^2 \Rightarrow a = 4 \text{ m/s}^2$

The velocity of the block at $t = 1 \text{ s}$ is:

$v = u + at = 0 + 4(1) = 4 \text{ m/s}$

The kinetic energy of the block at this instant is:

$K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}(2.0)(4)^2 = 16 \text{ J}$

Alternatively, using the work-energy theorem:

The component of gravitational force acting downwards along the incline is $mg \sin 37^\circ = 2.0 \times 10 \times \dfrac{3}{5} = 12 \text{ N}$.

Work done by gravity is $W_g = -mg \sin 37^\circ \times s = -12 \times 2 = -24 \text{ J}$.

The net work done on the block is $W_{\text{net}} = W + W_g = 40 - 24 = 16 \text{ J}$.

By the work-energy theorem, $\Delta K = W_{\text{net}} \Rightarrow K - 0 = 16 \text{ J}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $2.0 \text{ kg}$ is pushed down an inclined plane of inclination $37^\circ$ by a $20 \text{ N}$ force acting parallel to the incline. It is observed that the block travels on the incline with an acceleration of $10 \text{ m/s}^2$. Assuming the block starts from rest, determine the work done by the weight of the block during the first second. Take $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
The distance traveled by the block in the first second is given by the kinematic equation:

$s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$

Since the block starts from rest, $u = 0$. Substituting the given values $a = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$ and $t = 1 \text{ s}$:

$s = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2}(10)(1)^2 = 5 \text{ m}$

The weight of the block acts vertically downwards, and its component parallel to the inclined plane is $mg \sin \theta$. The work done by the weight of the block is the product of this parallel component and the displacement along the incline:

$W = (mg \sin \theta) \times s$

Substituting $m = 2.0 \text{ kg}$, $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$, $\theta = 37^\circ$, and $s = 5 \text{ m}$:

$W = (2.0 \times 10 \times \sin 37^\circ) \times 5$

Using $\sin 37^\circ = \dfrac{3}{5}$:

$W = 20 \times \dfrac{3}{5} \times 5 = 60 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $2.0 \text{ kg}$ is pushed down an inclined plane of inclination $37^\circ$ by a $20 \text{ N}$ force acting parallel to the incline. It is observed that the block travels on the incline with an acceleration of $10 \text{ m/s}^2$. Assuming the block starts from rest, determine the work done by the applied force during the first second. Take $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
Given initial velocity $u = 0$, acceleration $a = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$, and time $t = 1 \text{ s}$.

The displacement of the block in the first second is calculated using the equation of motion:

$s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$

$s = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2}(10)(1)^2 = 5 \text{ m}$

The applied force is $F = 20 \text{ N}$, acting parallel to the inclined plane in the direction of motion.

The work done by the applied force is:

$W = Fs$

$W = 20 \times 5 = 100 \text{ J}$

questions.q: A block of mass $2.0 \text{ kg}$ is pushed down an inclined plane of inclination $37^\circ$ by a $20 \text{ N}$ force acting parallel to the incline. It is observed that the block travels on the incline with an acceleration of $10 \text{ m/s}^2$. Assuming the block starts from rest, determine the work done by the frictional force acting on the block during the first second. Take $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
The displacement of the block in the first second is given by the equation of motion:

$s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$

Since the block starts from rest, $u = 0$. Substituting the given values $a = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$ and $t = 1 \text{ s}$:

$s = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2}(10)(1)^2 = 5 \text{ m}$

The forces acting on the block parallel to the inclined plane are the applied force $F$, the component of gravity $mg \sin \theta$, and the frictional force $f$ acting opposite to the motion. The equation of motion is:

$F + mg \sin \theta - f = ma$

Substituting $F = 20 \text{ N}$, $m = 2.0 \text{ kg}$, $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$, $\theta = 37^\circ$, and $a = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$20 + (2.0)(10) \sin 37^\circ - f = (2.0)(10)$

Using $\sin 37^\circ = \dfrac{3}{5}$:

$20 + 20 \left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right) - f = 20$

$20 + 12 - f = 20$

$f = 12 \text{ N}$

The work done by the frictional force is the product of the frictional force and the displacement. Since friction acts in the direction opposite to the displacement:

$W_f = -f \times s$

$W_f = -12 \times 5 = -60 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A $250 \text{ g}$ block slides on a rough horizontal table. Determine the work done by the frictional force in bringing the block to rest if it is initially travelling at a speed of $40 \text{ cm/s}$. If the friction coefficient between the table and the block is $0.1$, determine how far the block moves before coming to rest.
questions.solution:
Given mass of the block, $m = 250 \text{ g} = 0.25 \text{ kg}$
Initial velocity, $v = 40 \text{ cm/s} = 0.4 \text{ m/s}$
Final velocity, $v_f = 0 \text{ m/s}$

By the work-energy theorem, the work done by the frictional force is equal to the change in kinetic energy of the block:
$W = \Delta K = K_f - K_i$
$W = 0 - \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2$
$W = - \dfrac{1}{2} \times 0.25 \times (0.4)^2 = -0.02 \text{ J}$

The frictional force acting on the block is given by $f = \mu m g$.
Taking $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$,
$f = 0.1 \times 0.25 \times 9.8 = 0.245 \text{ N}$

The work done by friction is also given by $W = -f d$, where $d$ is the distance moved before coming to rest.
$-0.02 = -0.245 \times d$
$d = \dfrac{0.02}{0.245} \text{ m} \approx 0.0816 \text{ m} = 8.16 \text{ cm}$

Rounding to one decimal place, the distance is $8.2 \text{ cm}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Water descending from a $50 \text{ m}$ high fall is utilized to generate electric energy. If $1.8 \times 10^5 \text{ kg}$ of water falls per hour and half of the gravitational potential energy can be converted into electric energy, determine how many $100 \text{ W}$ lamps can be lit.
questions.solution:
Mass of water falling per second, $\dfrac{m}{t} = \dfrac{1.8 \times 10^5}{3600} = 50 \text{ kg/s}$

Total power available from the falling water is $P = \dfrac{mgh}{t}$

Taking $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$, we get:

$P = 50 \times 10 \times 50 = 25000 \text{ W}$

Electric power generated is half of the available power:

$P_{elec} = \dfrac{25000}{2} = 12500 \text{ W}$

Number of $100 \text{ W}$ lamps that can be lit is:

$n = \dfrac{12500}{100} = 125$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: While painting the walls of his house, a person stands on a ladder holding a bucket containing paint in one hand and a brush in the other. Suddenly, the bucket slips from his grasp and falls to the floor. If the bucket with the paint possessed a mass of $6.0 \text{ kg}$ and was at a height of $2.0 \text{ m}$ when it slipped, how much gravitational potential energy is lost together with the paint?
questions.solution:
The loss in gravitational potential energy is given by:

$\Delta U = mgh$

Substituting the given values $m = 6.0 \text{ kg}$, $h = 2.0 \text{ m}$, and $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$\Delta U = 6.0 \times 9.8 \times 2.0$

$\Delta U = 117.6 \text{ J}$

Rounding to the nearest integer, the lost gravitational potential energy is $118 \text{ J}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A projectile is launched from the top of a $40 \text{ m}$ high cliff with an initial speed of $50 \text{ m/s}$ at an unspecified angle. Determine its speed upon striking the ground.
questions.solution:
Using the principle of conservation of mechanical energy, the total energy of the projectile remains constant.

Let $m$ be the mass of the projectile. Taking the ground as the reference level for potential energy:

Initial energy $E_i = \dfrac{1}{2}mu^2 + mgh$

Final energy $E_f = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$

Equating initial and final energies:

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}mu^2 + mgh$

$v^2 = u^2 + 2gh$

Substituting the given values ($u = 50 \text{ m/s}$, $h = 40 \text{ m}$) and taking $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$v^2 = (50)^2 + 2(10)(40)$

$v^2 = 2500 + 800 = 3300$

$v = \sqrt{3300} \approx 57.4 \text{ m/s}$

The closest value among the given options is $58 \text{ m/s}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The $200 \text{ m}$ free style women's swimming gold medal at the Asian Games went to Priya of India when she established a new record of $1$ minute and $57.56$ seconds. Assuming she completed the majority of the distance at a uniform speed and was required to exert $460 \text{ W}$ to sustain her speed, determine the average force of resistance provided by the water during the swim.
questions.solution:
Distance $d = 200 \text{ m}$

Time $t = 1 \text{ min } 57.56 \text{ s} = 60 + 57.56 = 117.56 \text{ s}$

Average speed $v = \dfrac{d}{t} = \dfrac{200}{117.56} \text{ m/s}$

Power $P = 460 \text{ W}$

Since the speed is uniform, the force exerted by the swimmer equals the force of resistance provided by the water.

Using the relation $P = F \times v$, we get:

$F = \dfrac{P}{v} = \dfrac{P \times t}{d}$

$F = \dfrac{460 \times 117.56}{200} = 2.3 \times 117.56 = 270.388 \text{ N}$

The average force of resistance is approximately $270 \text{ N}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The athlete Emily Davis won the $100 \text{ m}$ sprint gold medal at London Olympic 2012 setting a new Olympic record of $10.54 \text{ s}$. Assume that she achieved her maximum speed in a very short time and subsequently ran the race with that speed till she crossed the line. Take her mass to be $50 \text{ kg}$. Calculate the kinetic energy of Emily Davis at her full speed.
questions.solution:
Given that the athlete achieved her maximum speed in a very short time and maintained it throughout the race, her speed can be considered constant.

The constant speed is given by:

$v = \dfrac{\text{Distance}}{\text{Time}} = \dfrac{100}{10.54} \approx 9.487 \text{ m/s}$

The kinetic energy $K$ of the athlete at her full speed is:

$K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$

Substituting the given values ($m = 50 \text{ kg}$):

$K = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 50 \times \left(\dfrac{100}{10.54}\right)^2$

$K = 25 \times 90.015 \approx 2250 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The athlete Emily Davis won the $100 \text{ m}$ sprint gold medal at London Olympic 2012 setting a new Olympic record of $10.54 \text{ s}$. Assume that she achieved her maximum speed in a very short time and subsequently ran the race with that speed till she crossed the line. Take her mass to be $50 \text{ kg}$. Assuming that the track, the wind etc. offered an average resistance of one tenth of her weight, calculate the work done by the resistance during the run.
questions.solution:
Mass of the athlete, $m = 50 \text{ kg}$

Acceleration due to gravity, $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$

Weight of the athlete, $W = mg = 50 \times 9.8 = 490 \text{ N}$

Average resistance force, $f = \dfrac{1}{10} W = \dfrac{1}{10} \times 490 = 49 \text{ N}$

Displacement of the athlete, $s = 100 \text{ m}$

Since the resistance force acts in the direction opposite to the displacement, the angle between them is $180^{\circ}$.

Work done by the resistance, $W_R = f s \cos(180^{\circ}) = -f s$

$W_R = -49 \times 100 = -4900 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The athlete Emily Davis won the $100 \text{ m}$ sprint gold medal at London Olympic 2012 setting a new Olympic record of $10.54 \text{ s}$. Assume that she achieved her maximum speed in a very short time and subsequently ran the race with that speed till she crossed the line. Take her mass to be $50 \text{ kg}$. Assuming that the track, the wind etc. offered an average resistance of one tenth of her weight, determine the power Emily Davis had to exert to maintain uniform speed.
questions.solution:
Given distance $s = 100 \text{ m}$ and time $t = 10.54 \text{ s}$.

Since the maximum speed is achieved in a very short time, the uniform speed of the athlete is:

$v = \dfrac{s}{t} = \dfrac{100}{10.54} \text{ m/s}$

The average resistance force offered by the track and wind is one-tenth of her weight. Taking $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$F = \dfrac{1}{10}mg = \dfrac{1}{10} \times 50 \times 9.8 = 49 \text{ N}$

To maintain a uniform speed, the athlete must exert a force equal to the resistance force. The power exerted by the athlete is:

$P = F \times v = 49 \times \dfrac{100}{10.54}$

$P = \dfrac{4900}{10.54} \approx 464.9 \text{ W}$

Rounding to the nearest integer gives $465 \text{ W}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A water pump extracts water from a depth $10 \text{ m}$ below the ground. The water is pumped up at a rate of $30 \text{ kg/minute}$ with negligible velocity. Determine the minimum horsepower the engine must possess to accomplish this.
questions.solution:
The work done by the pump in lifting water is equal to the change in potential energy of the water.

Given:
Mass of water pumped per minute, $m = 30 \text{ kg}$
Time, $t = 1 \text{ minute} = 60 \text{ s}$
Depth, $h = 10 \text{ m}$
Acceleration due to gravity, $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$

The power required in watts is given by:
$P = \dfrac{mgh}{t}$

Substituting the given values:
$P = \dfrac{30 \times 9.8 \times 10}{60} = 49 \text{ W}$

To convert the power into horsepower, we use the conversion $1 \text{ hp} = 746 \text{ W}$.

$P = \dfrac{49}{746} \text{ hp} \approx 0.066 \text{ hp}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An agitated protester lifts a stone of mass $200 \text{ g}$ from the ground and throws it at an opponent. At the instant of projection, the stone is $150 \text{ cm}$ above the ground and possesses a speed of $3.00 \text{ m/s}$. Determine the work done by the protester during this process. If the protester takes one second to lift and throw the stone, what horsepower is utilized?
questions.solution:
Mass of the stone, $m = 200 \text{ g} = 0.2 \text{ kg}$

Height of projection, $h = 150 \text{ cm} = 1.5 \text{ m}$

Speed of projection, $v = 3.00 \text{ m/s}$

Time taken, $t = 1 \text{ s}$

The work done by the protester is equal to the total mechanical energy imparted to the stone.

$W = \Delta K + \Delta U$

$W = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + mgh$

$W = \dfrac{1}{2}(0.2)(3.00)^2 + (0.2)(9.8)(1.5)$

$W = 0.9 + 2.94 = 3.84 \text{ J}$

Power utilized is the work done per unit time.

$P = \dfrac{W}{t} = \dfrac{3.84}{1} = 3.84 \text{ W}$

Since $1 \text{ hp} = 746 \text{ W}$, the power in horsepower is:

$P = \dfrac{3.84}{746} \text{ hp} \approx 5.14 \times 10^{-3} \text{ hp}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A factory requires an engine to lift $2000 \text{ kg}$ of metal through a distance of $12 \text{ m}$ in $1$ minute. Determine the minimum horsepower of the engine needed for this task.
questions.solution:
Work done by the engine to lift the metal is given by:

$W = mgh$

Substituting the given values ($m = 2000 \text{ kg}$, $h = 12 \text{ m}$, $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$):

$W = 2000 \times 9.8 \times 12 = 235200 \text{ J}$

The time taken is $t = 1 \text{ min} = 60 \text{ s}$.

Power $P$ is the rate of work done:

$P = \dfrac{W}{t} = \dfrac{235200}{60} = 3920 \text{ W}$

Converting the power into horsepower ($1 \text{ hp} = 746 \text{ W}$):

$P = \dfrac{3920}{746} \approx 5.25 \text{ hp}$

Using $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$, we get $P = \dfrac{2000 \times 10 \times 12}{60} = 4000 \text{ W}$, which gives $P = \dfrac{4000}{746} \approx 5.36 \text{ hp}$.

The closest value among the given options is $5.3 \text{ hp}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A scooter company provides the following specifications for its product:
Weight of the scooter — $95 \text{ kg}$
Maximum speed — $60 \text{ km/h}$
Maximum engine power — $3.5 \text{ hp}$
Pick up time to reach the maximum speed — $5 \text{ s}$
By evaluating the required power, what can be concluded about the validity of these specifications?
options: The specifications are valid, as the minimum average power required is less than the maximum engine power.
The specifications are underclaimed, as the minimum average power required is less than half of the maximum engine power.
The specifications are overclaimed, as the minimum average power required to accelerate the scooter exceeds the maximum engine power.
The specifications are valid, as the maximum engine power could achieve the maximum speed in under $3 \text{ s}$.
questions.solution:
First, we convert the maximum speed of the scooter from km/h to m/s:

$v = 60 \text{ km/h} = 60 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m/s} = \dfrac{50}{3} \text{ m/s}$

The kinetic energy of the scooter at this maximum speed is:

$K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 95 \times \left(\dfrac{50}{3}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 95 \times \dfrac{2500}{9} = \dfrac{237500}{18} \approx 13194.4 \text{ J}$

The minimum average power required to accelerate the scooter to this speed in $5 \text{ s}$ (ignoring air resistance and friction) is:

$P_{avg} = \dfrac{K}{t} = \dfrac{13194.4}{5} \approx 2638.9 \text{ W}$

Now, we convert the maximum engine power from horsepower to Watts (using $1 \text{ hp} = 746 \text{ W}$):

$P_{max} = 3.5 \text{ hp} = 3.5 \times 746 \text{ W} = 2611 \text{ W}$

Comparing the required average power and the maximum engine power:

$P_{avg} \approx 2638.9 \text{ W} > P_{max} = 2611 \text{ W}$

Since the minimum average power required to achieve the given specifications exceeds the maximum power the engine can produce, the specifications are overclaimed.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $30.0 \text{ kg}$ is lowered by a chain. Determine the work done by the chain if the block acquires a speed of $40.0 \text{ cm/s}$ after dropping down a distance of $2.00 \text{ m}$. (Take $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.solution:
Given $m = 30.0 \text{ kg}$, $h = 2.00 \text{ m}$, $v = 40.0 \text{ cm/s} = 0.40 \text{ m/s}$, and $u = 0$.

According to the work-energy theorem, the net work done on the block is equal to its change in kinetic energy:

$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$

$W_{\text{gravity}} + W_{\text{chain}} = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - \dfrac{1}{2}mu^2$

The work done by gravity is:

$W_{\text{gravity}} = mgh = 30.0 \times 9.8 \times 2.00 = 588.0 \text{ J}$

The change in kinetic energy is:

$\Delta K = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 30.0 \times (0.40)^2 = 15.0 \times 0.16 = 2.4 \text{ J}$

Substituting these values into the work-energy equation:

$588.0 + W_{\text{chain}} = 2.4$

$W_{\text{chain}} = 2.4 - 588.0 = -585.6 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an Atwood machine, the heavier block has a mass twice that of the lighter block. When the system is released from rest, the tension in the string is $16.0 \text{ N}$. Determine the decrease in gravitational potential energy during the first second of motion.
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the lighter block be $m$ and the heavier block be $2m$.

The acceleration of the system is $a = \dfrac{2m - m}{2m + m}g = \dfrac{g}{3}$.

The tension in the string is $T = \dfrac{2(2m)(m)}{2m + m}g = \dfrac{4mg}{3}$.

Given $T = 16.0 \text{ N}$, we have $\dfrac{4mg}{3} = 16.0 \Rightarrow mg = 12.0 \text{ N}$.

The distance moved by the blocks in the first second ($t = 1 \text{ s}$) is $s = \dfrac{1}{2}at^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{g}{3}\right)(1)^2 = \dfrac{g}{6}$.

The decrease in gravitational potential energy is $\Delta U = (2m)gs - mgs = mgs$.

Substituting the values, $\Delta U = (12.0)\left(\dfrac{g}{6}\right) = 2.0g$.

Taking $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$, $\Delta U = 2.0 \times 9.8 = 19.6 \text{ J}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An Atwood machine has two blocks of masses $2.0 \text{ kg}$ and $3.0 \text{ kg}$. Determine the work done by gravity during the fourth second after releasing the system from rest.
questions.solution:
The acceleration of the blocks in the Atwood machine is given by:

$a = \dfrac{m_2 - m_1}{m_1 + m_2} g$

Substituting the given masses $m_1 = 2.0 \text{ kg}$ and $m_2 = 3.0 \text{ kg}$:

$a = \dfrac{3.0 - 2.0}{3.0 + 2.0} g = \dfrac{g}{5}$

The displacement of the blocks during the $4^{\text{th}}$ second is:

$s_4 = u + \dfrac{a}{2}(2n - 1)$

$s_4 = 0 + \dfrac{g/5}{2}(2(4) - 1) = \dfrac{7g}{10}$

The net work done by gravity on the system is the sum of the work done on each block. Since the heavier block moves downwards and the lighter block moves upwards:

$W = m_2 g s_4 - m_1 g s_4 = (m_2 - m_1) g s_4$

$W = (3.0 - 2.0) g \left(\dfrac{7g}{10}\right) = \dfrac{7g^2}{10}$

Taking standard gravity $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$W = \dfrac{7 \times (9.8)^2}{10} = \dfrac{7 \times 96.04}{10} = 67.228 \text{ J}$

Rounding to the nearest integer, we get $W \approx 67 \text{ J}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Observe the setup illustrated in the figure. The system is released from rest, and the block of mass $1.0\text{ kg}$ is observed to possess a speed of $0.3\text{ m/s}$ after it has descended through a distance of $1\text{ m}$. Determine the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the table.
questions.solution:
Let $a_1$ and $v_1$ be the acceleration and velocity of the $1.0\text{ kg}$ block, and $a_2$ and $v_2$ be the acceleration and velocity of the $4.0\text{ kg}$ block.

From the constraint of the movable pulley, when the $1.0\text{ kg}$ block descends by a distance $h$, the $4.0\text{ kg}$ block moves by a distance $2h$. Thus, $v_2 = 2v_1$ and $a_2 = 2a_1$.

Given that the $1.0\text{ kg}$ block descends by $h = 1\text{ m}$ and attains a speed of $v_1 = 0.3\text{ m/s}$, we can find its acceleration using the kinematic equation:
$v_1^2 = u^2 + 2a_1 h$
$(0.3)^2 = 0 + 2a_1(1)$
$0.09 = 2a_1 \Rightarrow a_1 = 0.045\text{ m/s}^2$

The acceleration of the $4.0\text{ kg}$ block is:
$a_2 = 2a_1 = 2(0.045) = 0.09\text{ m/s}^2$

Let $T$ be the tension in the string. The $1.0\text{ kg}$ block is supported by two segments of the string, so the upward force is $2T$. Writing the equation of motion for the $1.0\text{ kg}$ block ($m = 1.0\text{ kg}$):
$mg - 2T = m a_1$
$1.0(10) - 2T = 1.0(0.045)$
$10 - 2T = 0.045 \Rightarrow 2T = 9.955 \Rightarrow T = 4.9775\text{ N}$

Writing the equation of motion for the $4.0\text{ kg}$ block ($M = 4.0\text{ kg}$), which is subjected to the tension $T$ and kinetic friction $f_k = \mu_k Mg$:
$T - \mu_k Mg = M a_2$
$4.9775 - \mu_k(4.0)(10) = 4.0(0.09)$
$4.9775 - 40\mu_k = 0.36$
$40\mu_k = 4.6175$
$\mu_k = \dfrac{4.6175}{40} \approx 0.1154$

Rounding to two decimal places, we get $\mu_k \approx 0.12$, which matches option (4).

The system is released from rest, and the block of mass $1.0\text{ kg}$ is observed to possess a speed of $0.3\text{ m/s}$ after it has descended through a distance of $1\text{ m}$. Determine the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the table.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a vertical plane, a closed circular tube of radius $10 \text{ cm}$ contains a block of mass $100 \text{ g}$ that just fits inside its cross-section. The block is propelled with a speed of $5.0 \text{ m/s}$ at the highest point of the tube. It executes multiple oscillations inside the tube before finally coming to rest at the lowest point. Determine the work done by the tube on the block during this process.
questions.solution:
Let the lowest point of the tube be the reference level for gravitational potential energy ($h = 0$).

At the highest point, the height of the block is $h = 2R = 2 \times 0.1 = 0.2 \text{ m}$.

The initial mechanical energy of the block is the sum of its kinetic and potential energies:

$E_i = K_i + U_i = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + mgh$

Substituting the given values ($m = 0.1 \text{ kg}$, $v = 5.0 \text{ m/s}$, $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$):

$E_i = \dfrac{1}{2}(0.1)(5.0)^2 + (0.1)(10)(0.2)$

$E_i = 1.25 + 0.20 = 1.45 \text{ J}$

The block finally comes to rest at the lowest point, so its final velocity is zero and its final height is zero.

The final mechanical energy is:

$E_f = K_f + U_f = 0 + 0 = 0 \text{ J}$

The work done by the tube on the block is equal to the work done by friction (since the normal force is perpendicular to the displacement and does zero work). By the work-energy theorem, the work done by non-conservative forces is equal to the change in the total mechanical energy of the block:

$W = \Delta E = E_f - E_i$

$W = 0 - 1.45 = -1.45 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A car weighing $1400 \text{ kg}$ is travelling up a hill at a speed of $54 \text{ km/h}$ when its motor stops. If it is just able to reach the destination which is at a height of $10 \text{ m}$ above the point, determine the work done against friction (the negative of the work done by friction). Assume $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
Mass of the car, $m = 1400 \text{ kg}$

Initial velocity, $u = 54 \text{ km/h} = 54 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m/s} = 15 \text{ m/s}$

Final velocity, $v = 0$

Height, $h = 10 \text{ m}$

Initial kinetic energy, $K_i = \dfrac{1}{2} m u^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1400 \times (15)^2 = 157500 \text{ J}$

Change in potential energy, $\Delta U = mgh = 1400 \times 9.8 \times 10 = 137200 \text{ J}$

By conservation of energy, the initial kinetic energy is used to increase the potential energy and do work against friction:

$K_i = \Delta U + W_{\text{against friction}}$

$157500 = 137200 + W_{\text{against friction}}$

$W_{\text{against friction}} = 157500 - 137200 = 20300 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small block of mass $200 \text{ g}$ is situated at the top of a frictionless incline which is $10 \text{ m}$ long and $3.2 \text{ m}$ high. Determine the work required to lift the block from the ground and place it at the top. Take $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
Mass of the block, $m = 200 \text{ g} = 0.2 \text{ kg}$

Height of the incline, $h = 3.2 \text{ m}$

Acceleration due to gravity, $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$

The work required to lift the block from the ground to the top of the incline is equal to the change in its gravitational potential energy.

$W = mgh$

$W = 0.2 \times 10 \times 3.2$

$W = 6.4 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small block of mass $200 \text{ g}$ is situated at the top of a frictionless incline which is $10 \text{ m}$ long and $3.2 \text{ m}$ high. Calculate the work required to slide the block up the incline. Take $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
Mass of the block, $m = 200 \text{ g} = 0.2 \text{ kg}$

Height of the incline, $h = 3.2 \text{ m}$

Length of the incline, $L = 10 \text{ m}$

Acceleration due to gravity, $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$

Since the incline is frictionless, the work done to slide the block up the incline slowly is equal to the change in its gravitational potential energy.

Alternatively, the force required to slide the block up the incline is $F = mg \sin \theta$, where $\sin \theta = \dfrac{h}{L}$.

Work done, $W = F \times L = mg \sin \theta \times L = mg \left( \dfrac{h}{L} \right) L = mgh$

$W = 0.2 \times 10 \times 3.2 = 6.4 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small block of mass $200 \text{ g}$ is situated at the top of a frictionless incline which is $10 \text{ m}$ long and $3.2 \text{ m}$ high. Determine the speed of the block when it reaches the ground if it falls off the incline and drops vertically to the ground. Take $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
By the principle of conservation of mechanical energy, the potential energy of the block at the top is converted entirely into kinetic energy when it reaches the ground.

$mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$

$v = \sqrt{2gh}$

Given that the height of the incline is $h = 3.2 \text{ m}$ and $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$, we substitute these values into the equation:

$v = \sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 3.2}$

$v = \sqrt{64} = 8.0 \text{ m/s}$

The mass of the block and the length of the incline are extraneous information.

questions.q: A small block of mass $200 \text{ g}$ is situated at the top of a frictionless incline which is $10 \text{ m}$ long and $3.2 \text{ m}$ high. Calculate the speed of the block when it reaches the ground if it slides down the incline. Take $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
Since the incline is frictionless, the mechanical energy of the block is conserved.

Loss in potential energy equals the gain in kinetic energy.

$mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$

$v = \sqrt{2gh}$

The speed is independent of the mass of the block and the length of the incline.

Substituting the given values $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$ and $h = 3.2 \text{ m}$:

$v = \sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 3.2}$

$v = \sqrt{64} = 8.0 \text{ m/s}$

questions.q: A slide in a park possesses a total length of $10 ext{ m}$ and a height of $8.0 ext{ m}$, as shown in the figure. A vertical ladder is provided to reach the top. A boy weighing $200 ext{ N}$ ascends the ladder to the upper end of the slide, then slides down to the ground. The slide offers an average friction equal to three tenths of his weight. Determine the work done by the boy on the ladder as he goes up. Neglect any work done by forces inside the body of the boy.
questions.solution:
The work done by a force is defined as the dot product of the force and the displacement of its point of application, $W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{s}$.

As the boy ascends, he applies a downward force on the steps of the ladder. However, the ladder is rigidly fixed to the ground and does not undergo any displacement.

Since the displacement of the point of application of the force is zero ($\vec{s} = 0$), the work done by the boy on the ladder is zero.

A boy weighing $200 	ext{ N}$ ascends the ladder to the upper end of the slide, then slides down to the ground. The slide offers an average friction equal to three tenths of his weight. Calculate the work done by the slide on the boy as he comes down. Neglect any work done by forces inside the body of the boy.
questions.solution:
Given:
Length of the slide, $s = 10 \text{ m}$
Weight of the boy, $W = 200 \text{ N}$
Average friction force, $f = \dfrac{3}{10}W = \dfrac{3}{10} \times 200 = 60 \text{ N}$

The slide exerts two forces on the boy: normal reaction and frictional force.

The work done by the normal reaction is zero because it is perpendicular to the direction of motion.

The work done by the frictional force is:
$W_f = -f \times s$
$W_f = -60 \times 10 = -600 \text{ J}$

Total work done by the slide on the boy is:
$W_{\text{slide}} = W_N + W_f = 0 - 600 = -600 \text{ J}$

A boy weighing $200 	ext{ N}$ ascends the ladder to the upper end of the slide, then slides down to the ground. The slide offers an average friction equal to three tenths of his weight. Find the work done by the ladder on the boy as he goes up. Neglect any work done by forces inside the body of the boy.
questions.solution:
Let the boy be considered as a point mass since the work done by internal forces is neglected.

The boy starts from rest at the bottom and comes to rest at the top, so the change in his kinetic energy is zero, $\Delta K = 0$.

The external forces acting on the boy are the downward force of gravity and the upward force exerted by the ladder.

The work done by gravity as the boy ascends a height $h = 8.0 \text{ m}$ is given by:

$W_{g} = -mgh$

Since the boy's weight is $mg = 200 \text{ N}$, the work done by gravity is:

$W_{g} = -200 \times 8.0 = -1600 \text{ J}$

Applying the work-energy theorem:

$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$

$W_{\text{ladder}} + W_{g} = 0$

$W_{\text{ladder}} - 1600 = 0$

$W_{\text{ladder}} = 1600 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: As depicted in the figure, a particle slides on a frictionless track that terminates in a straight horizontal section. If the particle begins slipping from point A, determine how far away from the track the particle will hit the ground.
questions.solution:
Let the initial height of the particle be $h_1 = 1.0\text{ m}$ and the height of the horizontal section of the track be $h_2 = 0.5\text{ m}$.

By the principle of conservation of mechanical energy, the velocity $v$ of the particle at the end of the track is given by:

$mg h_1 = mg h_2 + \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2$

$v = \sqrt{2g(h_1 - h_2)}$

Substituting the given values:

$v = \sqrt{2g(1.0 - 0.5)} = \sqrt{g}$

The particle leaves the track horizontally. The time $t$ taken to fall to the ground from height $h_2$ is:

$t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 h_2}{g}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(0.5)}{g}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{g}}$

The horizontal distance $x$ traveled by the particle from the edge of the track is:

$x = v \times t = \sqrt{g} \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{g}} = 1.0\text{ m}$

questions.q: As shown in the figure, a block weighing $10\text{ N}$ travels down a smooth curved track $AB$ connected to a rough horizontal surface. The coefficient of friction between the block and the rough surface is $0.20$. If the block begins slipping on the track from a point $1.0 \text{ m}$ above the horizontal surface, determine how far it will move on the rough surface.
questions.solution:
Given weight of the block, $W = mg = 10 \text{ N}$

Height of the track, $h = 1.0 \text{ m}$

Coefficient of friction, $\mu = 0.20$

By the work-energy theorem, the net work done on the block is equal to its change in kinetic energy.

Since the block starts from rest and finally comes to rest, the change in kinetic energy is zero, $\Delta K = 0$.

The work done by gravity as the block descends is:

$W_g = mgh = 10 \times 1.0 = 10 \text{ J}$

The work done by friction on the rough horizontal surface is:

$W_f = -\mu mg d = -0.20 \times 10 \times d = -2d$

Applying the work-energy theorem:

$W_g + W_f = \Delta K$

$10 - 2d = 0$

$2d = 10 \Rightarrow d = 5.0 \text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform chain having length $L$ and mass $M$ overhangs a horizontal table such that two-thirds of its length rests on the table. The friction coefficient between the table and the chain is $\mu$. Determine the work done by friction during the period the chain slips off the table.
questions.solution:
Let $x$ be the length of the chain on the table at any instant.

The mass of the chain on the table is $m = \dfrac{M}{L}x$.

The normal reaction on the chain is $N = mg = \dfrac{M}{L}xg$.

The frictional force acting on the chain is $f = \mu N = \mu \dfrac{M}{L}xg$.

When the chain slips by a small distance $ds$, the length of the chain on the table changes by $dx = -ds$.

The work done by friction during this small displacement is $dW = -f ds = f dx$.

Total work done by friction as the chain slips completely off the table is obtained by integrating from $x = \dfrac{2L}{3}$ to $x = 0$:

$W = \int_{\dfrac{2L}{3}}^{0} \mu \dfrac{M}{L}gx dx$

$W = \mu \dfrac{M}{L}g \left[ \dfrac{x^2}{2} \right]_{\dfrac{2L}{3}}^{0}$

$W = \mu \dfrac{M}{L}g \left( 0 - \dfrac{1}{2} \left( \dfrac{2L}{3} \right)^2 \right)$

$W = -\dfrac{2\mu MgL}{9}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform chain of mass $m$ and length $l$ overhangs a table with two-thirds of its length resting on the table. Determine the work to be done by a person to put the hanging portion back onto the table.
questions.solution:
Mass of the hanging portion of the chain is $m' = \dfrac{m}{3}$.

The center of mass of the hanging portion is at a depth $h = \dfrac{l/3}{2} = \dfrac{l}{6}$ below the edge of the table.

Work done to pull the hanging portion back onto the table is equal to the change in potential energy of the hanging portion.

$W = m'gh = \left(\dfrac{m}{3}\right)g\left(\dfrac{l}{6}\right) = \dfrac{mgl}{18}$

questions.q: A block of mass $1\text{ kg}$ is positioned at point $A$ on a rough track, as shown in the figure. When given a slight push to the right, it comes to rest at point $B$ on the track. Determine the work done by the frictional force on the block during its journey from $A$ to $B$.
questions.solution:
Using the work-energy theorem:

$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$

$W_{\text{gravity}} + W_{\text{friction}} = K_B - K_A$

Since the block starts from rest (given a slight push) and comes to rest at $B$, $K_A = 0$ and $K_B = 0$.

The work done by gravity is:

$W_{\text{gravity}} = mg(h_A - h_B)$

Substituting $m = 1\text{ kg}$, $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, $h_A = 1.0\text{ m}$, and $h_B = 0.8\text{ m}$:

$W_{\text{gravity}} = 1 \times 10 \times (1.0 - 0.8) = 2\text{ J}$

Therefore, the work-energy equation becomes:

$2 + W_{\text{friction}} = 0$

$W_{\text{friction}} = -2\text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $5.0 \text{ kg}$ is suspended from the end of a vertical spring, which stretches by $10 \text{ cm}$ under the load of the block. The block is delivered a sharp impulse from below, acquiring an upward speed of $2.0 \text{ m/s}$. How high will it rise? Take $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
At the equilibrium position, the spring force balances the weight of the block.

$k x_0 = mg$

$k (0.10) = 5.0 \times 10$

$k = 500 \text{ N/m}$

When the block is given an upward speed at the equilibrium position, it executes simple harmonic motion (SHM). The velocity at the equilibrium position is the maximum velocity of the SHM.

The angular frequency of the SHM is given by:

$\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{500}{5.0}} = 10 \text{ rad/s}$

The maximum height the block rises from the equilibrium position is equal to the amplitude $A$ of the SHM.

Using the relation $v_{\text{max}} = A \omega$:

$A = \dfrac{v_{\text{max}}}{\omega} = \dfrac{2.0}{10} = 0.20 \text{ m} = 20 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $250 \text{ g}$ is placed on a vertical spring with a spring constant of $100 \text{ N/m}$ that is fixed from below. The spring is compressed so its length is $10 \text{ cm}$ less than its natural length, and the system is released from this position. Calculate how high the block rises. Take $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
Let $h$ be the maximum height the block rises from its initial compressed position.

According to the law of conservation of mechanical energy, the initial elastic potential energy of the spring is converted into the gravitational potential energy of the block at the maximum height.

$\dfrac{1}{2}kx^2 = mgh$

Given:
$m = 250 \text{ g} = 0.25 \text{ kg}$
$k = 100 \text{ N/m}$
$x = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$
$g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$

Substituting the values into the energy equation:

$\dfrac{1}{2} \times 100 \times (0.1)^2 = 0.25 \times 10 \times h$

$50 \times 0.01 = 2.5h$

$0.5 = 2.5h$

$h = \dfrac{0.5}{2.5} \text{ m}$

$h = 0.2 \text{ m} = 20 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: As shown in the figure, a spring is fixed at the bottom end of an incline of inclination $37^\circ$. A small block of mass $2 \text{ kg}$ begins slipping down the incline from a point $4.8 \text{ m}$ away from the spring. The block compresses the spring by $20 \text{ cm}$, comes to a momentary halt, and subsequently rebounds through a distance of $1 \text{ m}$ up the incline. Determine the friction coefficient between the plane and the block. Take $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
Let the spring constant be $k$ and the coefficient of friction be $\mu$.

During the downward motion, the block starts from rest and comes to a momentary halt after compressing the spring. The total distance moved down the incline is $s_1 = 4.8 + 0.2 = 5.0 \text{ m}$.

Applying the work-energy theorem for the downward journey:
$W_{\text{gravity}} + W_{\text{friction}} + W_{\text{spring}} = \Delta K = 0$
$mg s_1 \sin 37^\circ - \mu mg s_1 \cos 37^\circ - \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2 = 0$
$\dfrac{1}{2}kx^2 = mg s_1 (\sin 37^\circ - \mu \cos 37^\circ)$ --- (1)

During the upward rebound, the block starts from rest at maximum compression and moves a distance $s_2 = 1.0 \text{ m}$ up the incline before coming to rest.

Applying the work-energy theorem for the upward journey:
$W_{\text{gravity}} + W_{\text{friction}} + W_{\text{spring}} = \Delta K = 0$
$-mg s_2 \sin 37^\circ - \mu mg s_2 \cos 37^\circ + \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2 = 0$
$\dfrac{1}{2}kx^2 = mg s_2 (\sin 37^\circ + \mu \cos 37^\circ)$ --- (2)

Equating (1) and (2):
$mg s_1 (\sin 37^\circ - \mu \cos 37^\circ) = mg s_2 (\sin 37^\circ + \mu \cos 37^\circ)$
$s_1 (\sin 37^\circ - \mu \cos 37^\circ) = s_2 (\sin 37^\circ + \mu \cos 37^\circ)$

Substituting $s_1 = 5.0 \text{ m}$, $s_2 = 1.0 \text{ m}$, $\sin 37^\circ = 0.6$, and $\cos 37^\circ = 0.8$:
$5.0 (0.6 - 0.8\mu) = 1.0 (0.6 + 0.8\mu)$
$3.0 - 4.0\mu = 0.6 + 0.8\mu$
$2.4 = 4.8\mu$
$\mu = \dfrac{2.4}{4.8} = 0.5$

Answer: $0.5$

questions.q: A spring is fixed at the bottom end of an incline of inclination $37^\circ$. A small block of mass $2 \text{ kg}$ begins slipping down the incline from a point $4.8 \text{ m}$ away from the spring. The block compresses the spring by $20 \text{ cm}$, comes to a momentary halt, and subsequently rebounds through a distance of $1 \text{ m}$ up the incline. Determine the spring constant of the spring. Take $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
Let the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline be $\mu$.

During the downward motion, the block travels a total distance $s_1 = 4.8 + 0.2 = 5 \text{ m}$ before coming to a momentary halt. Applying the work-energy theorem from the initial position to the point of maximum compression:

$W_{\text{gravity}} + W_{\text{friction}} + W_{\text{spring}} = \Delta K$

$mg s_1 \sin 37^\circ - \mu mg s_1 \cos 37^\circ - \dfrac{1}{2} k x^2 = 0$

Substituting $m = 2 \text{ kg}$, $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$, $s_1 = 5 \text{ m}$, $x = 0.2 \text{ m}$, $\sin 37^\circ = \dfrac{3}{5}$, and $\cos 37^\circ = \dfrac{4}{5}$:

$2 \times 10 \times 5 \times \dfrac{3}{5} - \mu \times 2 \times 10 \times 5 \times \dfrac{4}{5} = \dfrac{1}{2} k (0.2)^2$

$60 - 80\mu = 0.02k$

During the upward rebound, the block travels a distance $s_2 = 1 \text{ m}$ up the incline from the point of maximum compression. Applying the work-energy theorem for the upward journey:

$-mg s_2 \sin 37^\circ - \mu mg s_2 \cos 37^\circ + \dfrac{1}{2} k x^2 = 0$

Substituting the values with $s_2 = 1 \text{ m}$:

$-2 \times 10 \times 1 \times \dfrac{3}{5} - \mu \times 2 \times 10 \times 1 \times \dfrac{4}{5} + 0.02k = 0$

$-12 - 16\mu + 0.02k = 0$

$0.02k = 12 + 16\mu$

Equating the two expressions for $0.02k$:

$60 - 80\mu = 12 + 16\mu$

$48 = 96\mu \Rightarrow \mu = 0.5$

Substituting $\mu = 0.5$ into the equation for $k$:

$0.02k = 12 + 16(0.5)$

$0.02k = 20$

$k = \dfrac{20}{0.02} = 1000 \text{ N/m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $m$ travelling at a speed $v$ compresses a spring by a distance $x$ before its speed reduces to half. Determine the spring constant of the spring.
questions.solution:
According to the law of conservation of mechanical energy, the decrease in kinetic energy of the block is equal to the potential energy stored in the spring.

Initial kinetic energy of the block is $K_i = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$

Final kinetic energy of the block is $K_f = \dfrac{1}{2}m\left(\dfrac{v}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{8}mv^2$

Potential energy stored in the spring is $U = \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2$

Equating the change in kinetic energy to the potential energy:

$K_i - K_f = U$

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - \dfrac{1}{8}mv^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2$

$\dfrac{3}{8}mv^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2$

$k = \dfrac{3mv^2}{4x^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In the arrangement depicted in the figure, the system is released from rest while the spring is initially unstretched. Assuming the pulley is frictionless, determine the maximum elongation of the spring.
questions.solution:
Let the maximum elongation of the spring be $x$.

At the position of maximum elongation, the velocity of the block is zero. Therefore, the change in kinetic energy of the system is zero ($\Delta K = 0$).

As the block of mass $m$ moves downwards by a distance $x$, the string pulls the top end of the spring upwards by the same distance $x$. Since the bottom end of the spring is fixed to the ground, the spring gets stretched by $x$.

The loss in gravitational potential energy of the block is:
$\Delta U_g = -mgx$

The gain in elastic potential energy of the spring is:
$\Delta U_s = \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2$

According to the principle of conservation of mechanical energy:
$\Delta K + \Delta U_g + \Delta U_s = 0$

$0 - mgx + \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2 = 0$

Since $x \neq 0$ at maximum elongation, we can divide by $x$:
$mg = \dfrac{1}{2}kx$

$x = \dfrac{2mg}{k}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: As shown in the figure, a block of mass $m$ is connected to two unstretched springs having spring constants $k_1$ and $k_2$. The block is displaced towards the right by a distance $x$ and subsequently released. Determine the speed of the block when it passes through the indicated mean position.
questions.solution:
When the block is displaced by a distance $x$ towards the right, the left spring is stretched by $x$ and the right spring is compressed by $x$.

Both springs exert a restoring force in the same direction (towards the left). The total restoring force on the block is:

$F = -k_1 x - k_2 x = -(k_1 + k_2)x$

This shows that the two springs act as a parallel combination with an equivalent spring constant:

$k_{eq} = k_1 + k_2$

The potential energy stored in the system at the extreme position is:

$U = \dfrac{1}{2} k_{eq} x^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} (k_1 + k_2) x^2$

When the block passes through the mean position, its potential energy is zero and its kinetic energy is maximum. By the principle of conservation of mechanical energy:

$\dfrac{1}{2} m v^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} (k_1 + k_2) x^2$

$v^2 = \dfrac{k_1 + k_2}{m} x^2$

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{k_1 + k_2}{m}} x$

questions.q: As shown in the figure, a block of mass $m$ is sliding with a velocity $\vec{v}$ across a smooth horizontal surface when it encounters a long horizontal spring. The spring has a spring constant $k$ and is fixed at its other end. Determine the maximum compression of the spring. Also, will the velocity of the block be the same as $\vec{v}$ upon returning to the initial position shown?
questions.solution:
By the principle of conservation of mechanical energy, the kinetic energy of the block is completely converted into the elastic potential energy of the spring at the point of maximum compression.

$\dfrac{1}{2} m v^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} k x_{\text{max}}^2$

$x_{\text{max}}^2 = \dfrac{m v^2}{k}$

$x_{\text{max}} = v\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$

Since the surface is smooth, there is no loss of energy. When the block returns to its initial position, its speed will be the same as its initial speed $v$. However, velocity is a vector quantity. The block will be moving in the opposite direction, so its velocity will be $-\vec{v}$, which is not the same as the initial velocity $\vec{v}$.

Therefore, the maximum compression is $v\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$ and the velocity will not be the same.

questions.q: A small block of mass $100\text{ g}$ is pushed against a horizontal spring fixed at one end, compressing the spring by $5.0 \text{ cm}$ as shown in the figure. The spring constant is $100 \text{ N/m}$. Upon release, the block travels horizontally until it detaches from the spring. At what horizontal distance from the free end of the spring will it strike the ground, which is $2 \text{ m}$ below the spring?
questions.solution:
By the conservation of mechanical energy, the elastic potential energy of the spring is converted into the kinetic energy of the block when it detaches from the spring at its natural length:

$\dfrac{1}{2} k x^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2$

$v = x \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}}$

Substituting the given values $k = 100 \text{ N/m}$, $m = 100 \text{ g} = 0.1 \text{ kg}$, and $x = 5.0 \text{ cm} = 0.05 \text{ m}$:

$v = 0.05 \sqrt{\dfrac{100}{0.1}} = 0.05 \sqrt{1000} = 0.5\sqrt{10} \text{ m/s}$

The block travels horizontally and falls a vertical distance $h = 2 \text{ m}$. The time of flight $t$ is given by:

$h = \dfrac{1}{2} g t^2 \Rightarrow t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$

Taking $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 2}{10}} = \sqrt{0.4} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{10}} \text{ s}$

The horizontal distance traveled by the block from the free end of the spring is:

$R = v \times t = 0.5\sqrt{10} \times \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{10}} = 1 \text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Consider a light rod of length $l$ with its upper end clamped such that it is free to rotate. A small heavy block is attached to its lower end. What is the minimum horizontal velocity that must be imparted to the block for it to travel in a complete vertical circle?
questions.solution:
For a block attached to a light rod, the rod can provide both tension and compression. Thus, the rod will not slacken like a string.

To complete the vertical circle, the minimum velocity at the highest point can be zero, i.e., $v_{top} = 0$.

Using conservation of mechanical energy between the lowest and highest points:

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_{top}^2 + mg(2l)$

Substituting $v_{top} = 0$:

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = mg(2l)$

$v^2 = 4gl$

$v = 2\sqrt{gl}$

questions.q: As shown in the figure, two blocks $A$ and $B$, each having a mass of $320 \text{ g}$, are connected by a light string passing over a smooth light pulley. The horizontal surface on which block $A$ can slide is smooth. Block $A$ is attached to a spring of spring constant $40 \text{ N/m}$ whose other end is fixed to a support $40 \text{ cm}$ above the horizontal surface. Initially, the system is released to move from rest with the spring vertical and unstretched. Determine the velocity of block $A$ at the instant it breaks off the surface below it. Take $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$.
questions.solution:
Let $x$ be the horizontal displacement of block A when it breaks off the surface.

The length of the spring at this instant is $L = \sqrt{h^2 + x^2}$, where $h = 0.4 \text{ m}$ is the initial height of the spring.

The extension in the spring is $\Delta L = L - h$.

The spring force is $F_s = k(L - h)$.

The vertical component of the spring force is $F_y = F_s \cos\theta = k(L - h) \dfrac{h}{L} = kh\left(1 - \dfrac{h}{L}\right)$.

Block A breaks off the surface when the normal reaction $N$ becomes zero. At this instant, the vertical component of the spring force balances the weight of block A:

$F_y = m_A g$

$kh\left(1 - \dfrac{h}{L}\right) = m_A g$

Substituting the given values ($k = 40 \text{ N/m}$, $h = 0.4 \text{ m}$, $m_A = 0.32 \text{ kg}$, $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$):

$40 \times 0.4 \left(1 - \dfrac{0.4}{L}\right) = 0.32 \times 10$

$16 \left(1 - \dfrac{0.4}{L}\right) = 3.2$

$1 - \dfrac{0.4}{L} = 0.2 \Rightarrow \dfrac{0.4}{L} = 0.8 \Rightarrow L = 0.5 \text{ m}$

The extension in the spring is $\Delta L = 0.5 - 0.4 = 0.1 \text{ m}$.

The horizontal displacement of block A is $x = \sqrt{L^2 - h^2} = \sqrt{0.5^2 - 0.4^2} = 0.3 \text{ m}$.

Since block A and block B are connected by a string, block B moves downwards by the same distance $x = 0.3 \text{ m}$.

Applying the principle of conservation of mechanical energy to the system (Block A + Block B + Spring):

Loss in gravitational potential energy of block B = Gain in kinetic energy of the system + Gain in elastic potential energy of the spring

$m_B g x = \dfrac{1}{2}(m_A + m_B)v^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}k(\Delta L)^2$

Substituting the values ($m_B = 0.32 \text{ kg}$):

$0.32 \times 10 \times 0.3 = \dfrac{1}{2}(0.32 + 0.32)v^2 + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 40 \times (0.1)^2$

$0.96 = 0.32 v^2 + 20 \times 0.01$

$0.96 = 0.32 v^2 + 0.2$

$0.32 v^2 = 0.76$

$v^2 = \dfrac{0.76}{0.32} = 2.375$

$v = \sqrt{2.375} \approx 1.54 \text{ m/s}$

Answer: $1.54 \text{ m/s}$

questions.q: A light rod of length $l$ is rigidly attached to a small heavy block at one end and a hook at the other end, as shown in the figure. The system is released from rest while the rod is in a horizontal position. A fixed smooth ring is located at a depth $h$ below the initial position of the hook, and the hook catches into the ring as it reaches there. Determine the minimum value of $h$ required so that the block moves in a complete circle about the ring.
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the heavy block be $m$. Since the system is released from rest in a horizontal position, it undergoes pure translational motion downwards under gravity.

When the hook has fallen a depth $h$, the block has also fallen a depth $h$. The velocity of the system just before the hook catches the ring is given by:
$v = \sqrt{2gh}$ (directed vertically downwards)

When the hook catches the smooth ring, it acts as a fixed pivot. At this instant, the rod is horizontal, and the velocity of the block is perpendicular to the rod. The impulsive force from the ring acts at the pivot, so it exerts zero torque about the pivot. Therefore, the angular momentum of the block about the ring is conserved.

Let $\omega$ be the angular velocity of the rod just after the catch. Conserving angular momentum about the ring:
$mvl = ml^2\omega \implies \omega = \dfrac{v}{l}$

The kinetic energy of the block just after the catch is:
$K = \dfrac{1}{2}m(\omega l)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = mgh$

Since the block is attached to a light rigid rod, the condition for it to complete a vertical circle is that it must just reach the highest point of the circle. At the highest point, its velocity can be zero ($v_{top} \ge 0$).

The highest point of the circle is at a height $l$ above the horizontal level of the ring. The potential energy required to reach this highest point from the ring's level is $mgl$.

By conservation of mechanical energy:
$K \ge mgl$
$mgh \ge mgl$
$h \ge l$

Thus, the minimum value of $h$ required is $l$.

Answer: $l$

questions.q: The bob of mass $m$ of a resting pendulum is given a sharp hit, imparting a horizontal velocity of $\sqrt{10\,gl}$, where $l$ represents the pendulum's length. Determine the tension in the string when the string is horizontal.
questions.solution:
Let the initial velocity at the lowest point be $v_0 = \sqrt{10gl}$.

Using the principle of conservation of mechanical energy between the lowest point and the horizontal position:

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv_0^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + mgl$

Substituting the value of $v_0$:

$\dfrac{1}{2}m(10gl) = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + mgl$

$5mgl - mgl = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$

$v^2 = 8gl$

At the horizontal position, the tension in the string provides the necessary centripetal force. The weight of the bob acts vertically downwards and has no component along the horizontal string.

$T = \dfrac{mv^2}{l}$

Substituting $v^2 = 8gl$:

$T = \dfrac{m(8gl)}{l} = 8mg$

questions.q: The bob of mass $m$ of a resting pendulum is given a sharp hit, imparting a horizontal velocity of $\sqrt{10\,gl}$, where $l$ represents the pendulum's length. Determine the tension in the string when the bob is at its highest point.
questions.solution:
Let $u$ be the velocity at the lowest point and $v$ be the velocity at the highest point.

Using conservation of mechanical energy between the lowest and highest points:

$\dfrac{1}{2}mu^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + mg(2l)$

Given $u = \sqrt{10gl}$, substituting this yields:

$\dfrac{1}{2}m(10gl) = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + 2mgl$

$5mgl = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + 2mgl$

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = 3mgl \Rightarrow v^2 = 6gl$

At the highest point, both tension $T$ and weight $mg$ act downwards towards the center of the circular path. The equation for centripetal force is:

$T + mg = \dfrac{mv^2}{l}$

Substituting $v^2 = 6gl$:

$T + mg = \dfrac{m(6gl)}{l}$

$T + mg = 6mg$

$T = 5mg$

questions.q: A spring with natural length $h$ and spring constant $k$ has one end fixed to the ground. The opposite end is connected to a smooth ring of mass $m$ that can slide along a fixed horizontal rod at a height $h$, as shown in the figure. The system is released from rest when the spring initially makes an angle of $37^\circ$ with the vertical. Determine the speed of the ring at the instant the spring becomes vertical.
questions.solution:
Let the initial length of the spring be $L$. From the given geometry, the vertical height is $h$ and the spring makes an angle of $37^\circ$ with the vertical.

$L \cos 37^\circ = h$

$L = \dfrac{h}{\cos 37^\circ} = \dfrac{h}{4/5} = \dfrac{5h}{4}$

The initial extension in the spring is:

$x = L - h = \dfrac{5h}{4} - h = \dfrac{h}{4}$

The initial mechanical energy of the system consists only of the elastic potential energy of the spring (since the ring is released from rest and gravitational potential energy remains constant):

$E_i = \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}k\left(\dfrac{h}{4}\right)^2 = \dfrac{kh^2}{32}$

When the spring becomes vertical, its length is equal to the height $h$, which is its natural length. Thus, the final elastic potential energy is zero. The final mechanical energy is purely the kinetic energy of the ring:

$E_f = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$

By the principle of conservation of mechanical energy:

$E_i = E_f$

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{kh^2}{32}$

$v^2 = \dfrac{kh^2}{16m}$

$v = \dfrac{h}{4}\sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}}$

questions.q: The bob of mass $m$ of a resting pendulum is given a sharp hit, imparting a horizontal velocity of $\sqrt{10\,gl}$, where $l$ represents the pendulum's length. Determine the tension in the string when the string makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with the upward vertical.
questions.solution:
Let the lowest point of the pendulum be the reference level for potential energy.

Initial kinetic energy is given by:

$K_i = \dfrac{1}{2} m u^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} m (10gl) = 5mgl$

When the string makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with the upward vertical, it makes an angle of $\theta = 180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ$ with the downward vertical.

The height of the bob from the lowest point is:

$h = l - l \cos\theta = l(1 - \cos 120^\circ) = l(1 - (-0.5)) = 1.5l$

Using conservation of mechanical energy:

$K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$

$5mgl + 0 = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2 + mg(1.5l)$

$\dfrac{1}{2} m v^2 = 3.5mgl \Rightarrow v^2 = 7gl$

The equation of motion for the bob in the radial direction is:

$T - mg \cos\theta = \dfrac{mv^2}{l}$

Substituting the values of $\theta$ and $v^2$:

$T - mg \cos 120^\circ = \dfrac{m(7gl)}{l}$

$T - mg(-0.5) = 7mg$

$T + 0.5mg = 7mg$

$T = 6.5mg$
